chunks.text: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, called Chinese hibiscus, China rose, shoe flower or shoeblack plant, is a bushy evergreen shrub or small tree, typically 2.5-5 metres tall, with glossy, serrated, pointed ovate leaves and large, showy, five-petalled flowers around 10 cm across that in the wild/original form are red with prominent orange-tipped stamens fused into a central tube, though centuries of selective breeding have produced cultivars in white, yellow, orange, peach, pink, and even blue and purple, with single or fully double petal forms. Despite its scientific and common names, it is neither a true rose nor native to China — it has in fact never been found growing wild anywhere, and a 2024 molecular and morphological study concluded it most likely originated as a deliberate hybrid created by Pacific Islanders by crossing Hibiscus cooperi (native to Vanuatu) with Hibiscus kaute (native to Tahiti), two species whose native ranges are more than 4,000 km apart — a cross that could only have happened because Polynesian voyagers carried H. kaute with them as a useful 'canoe plant'. This makes it one of the clearer documented examples of very early, intentional long-distance plant breeding and transport. The plant is polyploid (carrying extra sets of chromosomes), which produces great and sometimes unpredictable variation between a parent and its offspring and is part of why hobbyist breeders have found it so rewarding to create new cultivars. Its uses span the practical and the symbolic: in parts of India petals were historically rubbed on leather to shine shoes (the direct source of the 'shoeblack plant' name), while in Indonesian and Malay the common name literally translates as 'shoe flower'; the petals also serve as a natural pH indicator, turning dark pink/magenta in acid and green in base, and flower extracts are used in commercial cosmetics as humectants and hair/skin conditioners. It is edible and used in salads in parts of the Pacific and brewed as a tea in several countries, and it carries deep religious significance in South Asia — red blooms are a standard offering in Hindu worship of the goddess Devi, and in Bengal specifically in Kali puja. It is the official national flower of Malaysia, where it is known as bunga raya; introduced to the Malay Peninsula as early as the 12th century and formally declared the national flower in 1960, its five petals are read as representing the five principles of the Rukun Negara (the national philosophy) and it appears on Malaysian currency. The species cannot survive temperatures much below 10°C, so in temperate climates it is strictly a greenhouse or container plant brought indoors for winter.

chunks.text: This regional database entry, compiled from Himalayan and South Asian ethnobotanical literature, frames Chinese hibiscus primarily through its traditional-medicine identity rather than its ornamental one, describing the flower in classical humoral terms as a 'sweet, astringent, cooling' plant part that folk and Ayurvedic-adjacent practice uses to check bleeding, soothe irritated mucous membranes and relax spasms — properties that align with, but are not the same as, the plant's independently documented use for hair conditioning and scalp care across the Indian subcontinent, where boiled or crushed hibiscus flowers and leaves remain a common home remedy to promote hair growth and reduce premature greying and hair fall. It is important to flag these as traditional, orally transmitted claims rather than clinically validated medical treatments; the database itself catalogues historical and folk usage rather than certifying efficacy. The entry is a useful reminder that across much of South and Southeast Asia the plant occupies a dual role that Western 'ornamental shrub' framings tend to miss — it is simultaneously a garden flower, a cosmetic ingredient, a minor food/beverage plant, and a staple of household folk medicine, often all within the same community at the same time.
